_readme: THE STRATEGY PLANNER'S FRAMEWORKS, AS DATA. To-do item 15.1, Decision 3 of
design/mockups/strategy-planner.html, ruled by Mike 2026-09-16: a framework is DATA
naming its capture shape, and is NEVER its own screen. That ruling stands and is the
reason this file exists.
🔴 SUPERSEDED BY MIKE'S REDIRECTION OF 2026-09-17 - READ THE CENSUS BEFORE ADDING A ROW.
design/PLANNING-TEMPLATE-CENSUS.md is the measured survey of his own decks, and
design/features/strategy-planner.md is the Brief. Three things this file used to say are
no longer true, and each one would send a new row to the wrong place:
1. THE SCOPE IS 52 CONCEPTS, NOT 45. The 45 was counted from ADV.0's index. Mike's
scoping ruling of 2026-09-17 counts the five decks' own contents tables and agendas:
Business Targets 5, Strategic Orientation 1 4, Strategic Orientation 2 18, Sales &
Marketing 16, Organisational Review 9. Census section 1 holds the breakdown.
2. 🔴 ADV.0 PLANNING OUTCOMES IS NEVER THE SOURCE OF A CONCEPT OR ITS TEXT. It is a
COPY of the decks' contents tables and it has drifted: four concepts missing from
its Strategic Orientation scope, and every Sales & Marketing page reference off by
one from page 12 onward. A deck's own table sits in the same file as the slides it
points at and cannot drift from them, so THE DECK IS THE SOURCE - census section 5,
and Decision A on design/mockups/strategy-session-menu.html, approved 2026-09-17.
The `helpsClientTo` values already in this file were taken from ADV.0 before that
ruling and are replaced by the concept index, not extended. Do not add more from it.
(ADV.0 keeps its real job: opening the session and defining the four Planning
Domains, which is what _planningDomainsReadme below is quoting.)
3. THE FIVE SHAPES BELOW ARE SUPERSEDED, AND TWO OF THEM ARE WRONG against Mike's own
fill-in tables: `quadrants` gives S.W.O.T one free-text box per quadrant where the
real table is four numbered lines in each of four blocks, and `buckets` renders the
8 Profit Levers as ideas under headings where the slide is an equation and the
template is seven aims with three task lines each. The real libraries are TWO -
about 21 TEACHING forms and 9 CAPTURE forms, because a concept is taught in one
form and captured in another. Census sections 2, 3 and 4 finding 6.
🔴 A NEW .vue FILE NAMED AFTER A FRAMEWORK IS STILL THE THING THAT RULING REFUSED. If a
framework will not fit a form, the answer is a new FORM - one more for all 52 - never a
component for that one framework.
🔴 THE CONCEPT TEXT IS NOT HERE, AND MUST NOT BE COPIED HERE. Each framework points at
a material in a domain support file via `material`, and the loader joins them. Those
summaries are authored, reach the AI, and are edited in one place; a second copy here
would drift from the first and nothing would fail. The three domain support files are
strategy-, sales-marketing- and staff-domain-support.json - two of the four Planning
Domains live outside the strategy file, which is why the loader reads across all three.
⚠ AND THREE OF THE FIVE ROWS BELOW POINT AT MATERIALS MIKE RULED OUT OF SCOPE on
2026-09-17 - strategy-profit-levers-blue-ocean, strategy-swot-pest and
strategy-porters-pine are three of the six named in census section 1 as tools for SELLING
a plan rather than making one, and none has a deck in design/planning-templates/. The
CONCEPTS are in scope (Porter's page 13, the 8 Profit Levers page 39, S.W.O.T in
Strategic Orientation 1 section 2); the coaching text they pull is what comes from the
wrong place, and the concept index is what replaces it.
WHAT IS HERE THAT IS NOWHERE ELSE: the capture SHAPE, and the per-field PROMPTS, which
are the deck's own words and are what make a framework a facilitated conversation
rather than an empty grid.
FIVE FRAMEWORKS, NOT FIFTY-TWO, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. Mike's ruling: 'Build the
machine and prove it on three frameworks, not fifty.' They were chosen because they need
genuinely DIFFERENT shapes - if one renderer carries them, the rest are data entry.
SHAPES, ALL FIVE BUILT: buckets (sort ideas under named headings), quadrants (exactly
four boxes), forces (five or six, one marked centre), statements (a short list side by
side) and actions (a rows x columns table the loader expands into ordinary fields).
See point 3 above before reusing any of them.
TWO TEXTS PER FRAMEWORK, AND THEY ARE NOT DUPLICATES. 'explores' is the deck's own
Session Scope line for screen 1; the long coaching summary is JOINED from the domain
support file and shown on the framework card. A client choosing the scope and an advisor
running the session need different sentences. Mike ruled this 2026-09-16.
_planningDomainsReadme: THE FOUR PLANNING DOMAINS ARE THE SESSION - Mike's ruling. Their order and their
descriptions are ADV.0 Planning Outcomes' own words, from 'The Planning Domains
Explained'. They are NOT the app's advisory domains: a Planning Domain draws its
frameworks from whichever advisory domain authored them, which is why the loader reads

planningDomains.name: Business Targets
planningDomains.description: Revenue, profit and personal income targets, debt ratio and risk tolerance, work hours and leave expectations, and the specific focus areas the owner believes need attention.

planningDomains.name: Strategic Orientation
planningDomains.description: A challenging review of the actual business model — revenue streams, application of assets, target market — supported by external insights data and scenario modelling.

planningDomains.name: Organisational Review
planningDomains.description: Communication and reporting channels, divisional roles and individual responsibilities, in order to improve efficiencies and team engagement.

planningDomains.name: Sales & Marketing Review
planningDomains.description: How you attract attention to your product or service, how you convert attention into interest and action, and how you finally secure their custom.

_decksReadme: THE FIVE DOCUMENTS THE SESSION SCOPE MENU DRAWS AS PANELS - four Planning Domains
across five decks, because Strategic Orientation is ONE domain in TWO decks and only
the second of them carries a scope table. The menu groups by DECK, not by domain.
THE ORDER IS MIKE'S OWN and it is this array's order, never a sort. It puts the two
agenda-only documents first, which is deliberate: hiding them behind the richer decks
would make the screen look better than it is. Approved drawing, section 1.
A DECK IS NOT A DOMAIN AND MUST NOT BE COLLAPSED INTO ONE. Pivot.pdf - the acceptance
test - takes nine concepts from strategic-orientation-2 and two from sales-marketing,
so a menu that groups by domain would put nine of them under one heading with the
other deck's four agenda rows, which is not the table Mike's clients read.
sourceLabel says where the rows came from, in the deck itself. It is OUR provenance
note, not Mike's wording, and it is data rather than a locale string because it is a
fact about one deck. The rows' own text is his and lives on the concepts.
There is no rowSource field on purpose: whether a deck is an agenda or a scope table is
already on every concept, and the loader derives it and refuses a deck whose concepts

decks.name: Strategic Orientation 1
decks.sourceLabel: the agenda, slide 2 — it has no contents table

frameworks.name: The 8 Profit Levers
frameworks.helpsClientTo: Identify the little things that can contribute to massive business growth.
frameworks.captureInstruction: If you're running short of time you can identify just one task per lever for now; do the rest when time provides.

model.note: Decision 5, RULED AGAINST THE RECOMMENDATION: this runs INSIDE the framework card on the same backend route as the standalone page. Seamless is the surface, never a second copy of the maths.

fields.label: Number of Foot-traffic
fields.prompt: Gain their ATTENTION — market attention, outbound message views.

fields.label: Number of Prospects
fields.prompt: Capture their INTEREST — shop walk-ins, phone-ins or social click-thru.

fields.label: Number of Customers
fields.prompt: Secure their CUSTOM — the percentage of prospects that become customers.

fields.label: Average Customer Spend
fields.prompt: Secure their CUSTOM — total sales value divided by total number of transactions.

fields.label: Average Customer Frequency
fields.prompt: Keep them WANTING MORE — how often do they buy per month or year.

fields.label: Sales Margin
fields.prompt: Buy materials or stock FOR LESS — the difference between how much you sell it for and what it cost you.

fields.label: Activity Driven Costs
fields.prompt: Reduce SPENDING — the cost of gaining a customer.

fields.label: Fixed Costs (Overheads)
fields.prompt: Reduce SPENDING/OVERHEADS — the total regular cost of being open for business, even when nobody buys.

frameworks.explores: The accumulative effect of incremental changes in business activities.

frameworks.name: SWOT / PEST
frameworks.helpsClientTo: Establish a baseline of where they actually stand before anything is planned.
frameworks.captureInstruction: You don't have to complete them in any set order — just record them as they come to mind.

fields.label: Strengths
fields.prompt: Internal — personnel roles, communication lines, POS report accuracy, profit lines, technology usage.

fields.label: Weaknesses
fields.prompt: Internal — growth drag, and the financial instruments used to reduce risk.

fields.label: Opportunities
fields.prompt: External (PEST) — political, economic, interest rate, consumer confidence, regulatory or tariff changes.

fields.label: Threats
fields.prompt: External (PEST) — the same prompts, read the other way.

frameworks.explores: Internal position through strengths and weaknesses; the external macro-environment through political, economic, regulatory and tariff movement.

frameworks.name: Porter's 5 Forces
frameworks.helpsClientTo: Look out for changes in the market and anticipate how everyone will react, so they can be ready to take advantage of the situation.
frameworks.captureInstruction: You don't have to follow any particular order; just capture your thoughts as you go.

fields.label: Customers
fields.prompt: Are customers likely to be motivated to pay premium prices in return for latest style or fashion, technology or prestige? Are they concerned about your business safety, environment or ethical impact?

fields.label: New Entrants
fields.prompt: How easy is it for new entrants to enter your marketplace? Is it conceivable that your current supplier could become your future competition?

fields.label: Suppliers
fields.prompt: Is there competition amongst your suppliers? Do they actively compete for your business, and if you had to shift to a new supplier, how easy would it be?

fields.label: Substitutes
fields.prompt: What are the alternatives to your product or service? Could your customers solve their problem a different way?

fields.label: Existing Rivalry
fields.prompt: The centre of the model — what the other four press upon.

frameworks.explores: How customer trends, supplier tactics, new entrants and substitute products can all impact your business at the same time.

frameworks.name: Strategic Objective and Strategy
frameworks.helpsClientTo: Agree one desired end result, and the ethos that will get them there.
frameworks.captureInstruction: You can complete this here or as part of Strategic Orientation part 2 — it is the exact same table.

fields.label: Strategic Objective
fields.prompt: The desired end result — SINGULAR — inclusive of ongoing management plans.

fields.label: Strategy
fields.prompt: The ethos or belief about how best to achieve it. Effectively an acid test for every decision that follows.

frameworks.explores: The planning language itself: a singular desired end result, and the ethos that will reach it.

frameworks.name: Operational Objectives and Tactics
frameworks.helpsClientTo: Turn the session into things that are actually done, by someone, by a date.
frameworks.captureInstruction: ALL must pass the test: observable or measurable, bound by a timeframe, and clearly in support of the singular Strategic Objective.
_rowsNote: SIX ROWS IS A FIRST CUT, NOT A LIMIT ON PLANNING. The deck's own Action Plan Reminder is
a fixed table, and the loader expands `rows` x `columns` into ordinary fields so the store,
the timeline and the audit trail need no special case. Changing 6 to 12 is a data edit.

columns.label: Operational Objective
columns.prompt: Observable, time-bound, and in support of the Strategic Objective.

frameworks.explores: The things we want to achieve, turned into a task, a person and a date.

_exploresReadme: EXPLORES IS THE DECK'S OWN SESSION SCOPE LINE, and it is NOT the coaching summary.
Mike ruled 2026-09-16, comparing the build against the approved drawing: the Session Scope
table shows ONE SHORT LINE per framework, because a domain holding fifteen of them is
unreadable otherwise. The long coaching summary stays joined from the domain support file
and is shown on the framework CARD, where the advisor reads it while running the session.
Two sentences for two readers - a client choosing the scope, and the advisor running it.
This is NOT duplication, and neither may be deleted in favour of the other.
_conceptsReadme: THE CONCEPT INDEX - THE 52, AS RECORDS. To-do item 15.1. This is the thing the Planner
never had: a concept as a record of its own. Before it, the engine knew Strategic
Orientation 2 as ONE row and its eighteen concepts only as words inside that row, so a
ranker could not return a concept because no concept existed to return.
🔴 EVERY WORD OF `name`, `conceptSummary` AND `helpsClientTo` IS MIKE'S OWN, READ OFF HIS
DECKS BY MACHINE. Decision A, approved 2026-09-17: the menu IS his Session Scope table and
its words are never rewritten, summarised or generated. The 34 rows with text come from the
Session Scope tables of Strategic Orientation 2 (slides 3-5) and Sales & Marketing (slides
2-3). Ligatures are normalised to ASCII and nothing else is altered. If a sentence here
reads oddly, it reads that way on the slide - fix the deck, never this file.
WHERE EACH ROW CAME FROM, and why the count is 52:
session-scope-table  34  Strategic Orientation 2 (18) + Sales & Marketing (16)
agenda               18  Business Targets (5) + Strategic Orientation 1 (4) +
Organisational Review (9) - these decks have no scope table
🔴 A NULL DESCRIPTION IS DELIBERATE - Decision B, approved 2026-09-17. Where
conceptSummary or helpsClientTo is null, MIKE WRITES THAT LINE. It is never to be
generated, inferred from the slides, or filled in by an AI. A null means "not written
yet", never "this concept has no description".
THE ONE EXCEPTION IS HIS OWN, ruled 2026-09-17. Organisational Review's agenda already
prints a one-line description under each of its nine items - "Who reports to who?",
"What's MOST important to us?" - so those nine carry it as their conceptSummary. Like
every other line here it was READ OFF THE SLIDE by machine, not typed. That leaves
9 agenda rows still name-only (Business Targets 5, Strategic Orientation 1 4), and
ALL 18 still have a null helpsClientTo, which stays his.
🔴 SHARED TEXT IS STORED ONCE AND POINTED AT - Decision E, approved 2026-09-17. The decks
merge some table cells across two rows, so a `conceptSummaryRef` / `helpsClientToRef` names
the concept that HOLDS the text instead of copying it. Two copies drift, which is exactly
what ADV.0's index did. The three in the decks today:
price-for-delivery-medium  -> price-for-problem-solving  (both columns; one sentence
written across the pair, and they share the page-20 cell)
horizontal-integration     -> vertical-integration       (Helps column, one cell across both)
drafting-tender-proposals  -> its own conceptSummary     (the deck puts the same sentence
in both columns of that one row)
AN EDITING SCREEN MUST SAY WHICH ROWS SHARE A PIECE OF TEXT BEFORE ANYONE CHANGES IT, or
one row's edit silently rewrites its neighbour.
FORMS: `teachingForm` is how the SLIDE draws the concept; `captureForm` is the table the
client fills in. They are different things - census section 4 finding 6: nothing is ever
filled in as a ring, a staircase or a curve. Both come from PLANNING-TEMPLATE-CENSUS.md
section 3, which a PERSON produced by looking at the slides; a text extract cannot see a
picture, so these can never be machine-derived.
🔴 `captureFormBasis` IS NOT DECORATION. "measured" means the census matched this concept
to one of Mike's own fill-in templates, named in `captureTemplate`, so the assignment is
checkable. "unmeasured" means it did not, and census section 4 is explicit that CHOOSING a
capture form for such a concept is a DESIGN DECISION rather than a reading. They are left
null deliberately. Filling one in silently is this file designing the product.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: no concept carries its teaching or capture LAYOUT, because how
each form is drawn is undesigned (census section 7). No concept carries a screen.
⚠ THERE IS NO EXTRACTOR IN THIS REPOSITORY, AND THIS FILE IS NOW THE SOURCE. The rows were
read off the PDFs once, on 2026-09-17, by a throwaway script that was NOT kept: it is Python,
and this repository is JavaScript only under the Stack Constitution, so committing it would
have been a stack deviation needing its own reconcile task. tests/unit/strategyConcepts.test.js
PINS this data - it does not re-derive it. Re-extracting is a fresh task with its own tooling
decision, and design/features/strategy-planner.md section 8 lists the five traps that extraction
hit, so nobody meets them twice. The audit trail is the decks themselves, in
design/planning-templates/, plus design/PLANNING-TEMPLATE-CENSUS.md. The Brief is
design/features/strategy-planner.md.

concepts.name: Porter’s 5 Forces
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores how Customer Trends, Supplier Tactics, New Entrants and New Substitute/Alternative products can all impact your business at the same time.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To look out for changes in the market and anticipate how everyone will react; so you can be ready to take advantage of the situation.

concepts.name: Product Fit Review
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept examines the market/customer resistance by clarifying the major purchasing obstacles and competitor comparison.
concepts.helpsClientTo: By challenging the assumptions around customer demand for BOTH the problem to be solved - AND - the manner in which it is solved by your product/service - VS that of competitors.

concepts.name: Progression of Economic Value
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the ‘Business Imperatives’ that relate to each stage of the value chain and suggests that the ‘bright new thing’ becomes the ‘minimum standard’ in the future.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To identify what to focus on, depending on how they ‘add value’ to their customer.

concepts.name: Price For Problem Solving
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept Identifies the various pricing components in your service delivery (as they relate) to the value client’s place on their problem being solved.
concepts.helpsClientTo: This allows for a leveraged (delegated) team delivery AND multiple price points. Clients with more time (to do things themselves) can save money; those that just want the ‘problem to disappear’ can pay a premium for time saving and risk reduction.

concepts.name: Vertical Integration
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the supply and distribution chain to see if you need to own more of the value chain components.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To identify asset purchases or alliances that could help protect existing market share and sales margin or new products that could increase your sales.

concepts.name: Horizontal Integration
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the additional products or service that you could cross-sell to existing customers or would attract new customers to your business.

concepts.name: Market Diffusion Theory
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the introduction of a new product (similar to product life cycle) but focuses on how the market reacts and the ‘tipping point’ required to achieve success.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To identify where they are in the marketing process so they don’t waste money in the wrong areas. (kind of like the law of diminishing return / flogging a dead horse)

concepts.name: Boston Model
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept assists in the understanding of market position in terms of pricing, clientele & market acceptance. Originally designed to identify business divisions that should be sold, this model can be applied for both sale & growth discussions.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Stop and think about how the business/ product is positioned against competitors and determine if this is by direct strategy or failure to execute tactics.

concepts.name: Product Life Cycle
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores how a new product or service becomes popular (gains acceptance) and then over time, becomes outdated and no longer relevant. (Decline)
concepts.helpsClientTo: Understand the likelihood of your client’s product or service being replaced (or eroded) by new product offers, new technology or product substitutes.

concepts.name: Technology Points
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores how a product goes through stages of finding the right price point to improve market acceptance; how the cost of production comes down as sales volumes go up; that increased sales often result in lower sales prices and that eventually, big name brands will drop out and move to the next new thing.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To identify the ‘forces at play’ surrounding their product (or service) and to identify the opportunities (and threats) that could emerge in future. (Luck is often defined by preparation and timing)

concepts.name: Sigmoid Curve
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the natural ‘highs and lows’ of a product and to identify the signs that it’s time to make change. It also suggests the time to invest in new ideas is while you’re still enjoying positive cash flow from your existing product.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Look ahead and plan the investment/ improvement / development of your product now, BEFORE sales are dropping and you don’t have the cash to afford the necessary changes.

concepts.name: Blue Ocean Strategy
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores how you can attract customers that wouldn’t normally purchase your services or product.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To explore ways to make your business, product or service stand out from all your other competitors.tion Point’.

concepts.name: Revenue Streams
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores using unrelated products to increase foot traffic or shorter sales cycle offerings, vs related upsell or ‘after sale’ offerings.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Help your client to explore possible revenue alternatives or ways to diversify, whilst minimizing risk.

concepts.name: Risk Reward Matrix
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the idea that risk can be categorised into ‘Knowns, ‘Partial Unknowns’ and ‘Complete Unknowns’.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Identify new opportunities relating to market expansion and product diversification by only testing one ‘unknown’ at a time.

concepts.name: E. Deming’s Volatility Theory
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explains how Volatility can be measured in terms of Probability and therefore, can be a better ‘predictor’ of events going forward.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Develop more meaningful targets and reports.

concepts.name: Senge’s Circles of Causality
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept reminds us of how the ‘equal and opposite reaction’ law (in Physics), applies to business improvement also.
concepts.helpsClientTo: To expect the negative consequences in advance so they don’t get confused and change their plans (when they should have kept going)

concepts.name: The 8 Profit Levers
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explains the Accumulative effect of Incremental changes in business activities.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Identify the ‘little things’ that can contribute to massive business growth.

concepts.name: 6 Marketing Questions
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores 6 key questions to ensure you’ve considered your value from the customer’s perspective.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Get clear in your own mind about who you serve, how you add value and what makes you special. (Know what matters)

concepts.name: Product Fit
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the ‘trade-offs’ between business profitability and customer acceptance.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Increase sales conversions from the marketing leads you generate. (Even your sub-standard salespeople should be able to win sales with your product or service.)

concepts.name: 10 Marketing Messages
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores 10 marketing statements that ‘speak’ to the purchase decision points of your customer.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Convert what you’ve defined (in the marketing questions) into ‘sticky’ outbound marketing messages. (Know how to explain it to others)

concepts.name: Customer (Persona) Type Table
concepts.conceptSummary: This table summarises your customer types - to product fit.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Identify the ‘specific messaging’ for customer types vs the ‘general messaging’ for wider market coverage.

concepts.name: A.I.D.C.R.A Advertisement Framework
concepts.conceptSummary: This framework explains the logical order to construct an advertisement.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Build more effective adverts and have a review framework so you can ‘A’ and ‘B’ test if desired.

concepts.name: Digital Funnel Storyboard
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores the sequential offerings, messaging and responses, to entice your target customer ‘from their couch to your cash register’.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Get clear on how to utilise all their marketing assets in one comprehensive plan.

concepts.name: (Outbound) Messaging Plan
concepts.conceptSummary: This framework helps you schedule your messaging activities and explores Medium, Platform, Time & Cost as planning considerations.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Execute an effective campaign amongst all other business activities/ responsibilities.

concepts.name: (Inbound) Landing Page Review
concepts.conceptSummary: This framework defines the reader’s logic and the landing page logic, to help you define the sequence of text, graphics & widgets.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Build an effective landing page to convert more of your marketing leads into sales opportunity.

concepts.name: Sparketing (Friction) Review
concepts.conceptSummary: This concept explores a review of your product from a ‘what stops people from buying it?’ vs features/ profitability.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Get clear of what your customer will happily pay for, what they could care less about & what they just don’t want from you. 2

concepts.name: Branding Review
concepts.conceptSummary: This checklist helps you align your logo, graphics, message, market promise and ‘story’ so that you ‘stick’ in your customers mind.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Build powerful mental associations that create lasting influence in the mind of your target customer.

concepts.name: Customer Loyalty Programme
concepts.conceptSummary: This checklist helps to clarify the purpose of your customer loyalty programme and ensure it translates into profits for your business.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Stop giving stuff away if it doesn’t make a measurable improvement in your business profits.

concepts.name: Pricing
concepts.conceptSummary: This checklist encourages a review of your pricing beyond just ‘lifting it up’ or ‘dropping it down’. Your price should be an active reflection of the value you provide your customer.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Money is an exchange of value; you need to be clear on the value you offer to price in a sustainable fashion.

concepts.name: Packaging/ Bundling
concepts.conceptSummary: This checklist guides you through a review of how your packaging supports your ‘big promise’ and client perception.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Use packaging and bundled solutions to influence the purchasing decision, price point and quality perceptions of your product/ service.

concepts.name: Sales Channel Options
concepts.conceptSummary: This checklist explores the different sales channel options and encourages a pros and cons discussion.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Identify a variety of ways to engage salespeople to sell your products or service to a wider market.

concepts.name: Sales Process Review
concepts.conceptSummary: These templates encourage a review of the sales process from both customer and salesperson perspectives.
concepts.helpsClientTo: Know what to say and when to ‘say it’ to help a customer choose to do business with you.

concepts.name: Drafting Tender Proposals
concepts.conceptSummary: Just a few notes/ ideas to incorporate in your tender applications as you see fit. (General reading rather than focused session)

concepts.name: Determine Your Business Development Stages (Profile Points)
Choose Your Objectives (what you want to achieve)
Review Your Profit Lever Focus (how you plan to achieve your objectives - based on the profit levers)
Plan your meeting follow-up (using the client plan feature)
Review the Planning Process & Language to ensure we’re all on the ‘same page’. (section 1)
Assess current position by reviewing (pre-meeting) data (section 2) & Financial Performance Reports
Determine the business Strategic Objective & document the Strategy (section 3)
Brainstorm & record Operational Objectives and Tactics (actions) in the Automated Action Plan Reminder
Review the Development Stages of the Organisation

concepts.conceptSummary: What our team say about the organisation

concepts.conceptSummary: Are we doing the basics (already) before seeking improvement?

concepts.name: Define the Leadership Style Necessary for Success
concepts.conceptSummary: How best to lead our team

concepts.name: Define the Cultural Core Values
concepts.conceptSummary: What’s MOST important to us?

concepts.name: Understanding our Habit Drivers
concepts.conceptSummary: Why we do the same old things, the same old way

concepts.name: Design the Organisational Hierarchy Chart
concepts.conceptSummary: Who reports to who?

concepts.name: Determine the Divisional KPI’s
concepts.conceptSummary: How we measure divisional performance

concepts.name: Develop Cascaded Operational Objectives
concepts.conceptSummary: Milestones, broken down to each team layer
